source.title: WSC339 CW2 · Circuit design (Part 2), Loughborough University
source.note: The student's own coursework: Q1 lumped L-network, Q2 short-circuit stub (two positions on a 15 cm line), Q3 lumped replacement of the stubs, Q4 signal-flow graph. No official answers: every number is a claim, checked here. The MWO markers in the student's screenshots (Graphs 2a, 2b, 3a, 3b) are an independent simulator and are used as test cases. Also ingested: lab1 post-lab (CW1, slotted-line VSWR lab), whose answers are checked in truth.mjs; the AWR scheduler logs and project files carry no data.

assumptions: Ideal lossless TEM lines with Eeff = 1 (vp = c), exactly as the coursework's MWO TLINP blocks.
The antenna is a ZFREQ block: 72 + j100 Ω at every frequency, as in the coursework's schematics. A real antenna's impedance would also move with frequency; the game says so.
λ at 2 GHz = c / f = 14.99 cm; the coursework rounds it to 15 cm, so the 15 cm line is one wavelength.

concepts.title: Γ = (ZL − Z0)/(ZL + Z0), VSWR and the standing wave
With r > 1 the shunt element must sit at the load
Series parts move along constant-r circles, shunt parts along constant-g circles
Element values from normalised steps: L = Z0/(ω|b|), C = 1/(ω|x|Z0)
Moving along a line rotates Γ on the VSWR circle: Γ(d) = ΓL·e^(−j2βd)
A shorted stub adds −j·cot(βℓ): short = inductive, past λ/4 = capacitive
Matching is narrowband; the stub closest to the load has the widest band
Zsc = jZ0·tan(βℓ) gives the lumped equivalent at one frequency

misconceptions.text: 72 Ω is close to 50 Ω, so the antenna is nearly matched (the +j100 is ignored).
Either element can go first in an L-network.
Any added reactance moves the point the same way on the chart.
There are only two places a stub can go.
A deeper dip at 2 GHz means a better match (the coursework's own choice of stub B).
Stub positions repeat every λ/2, so they are all equivalent.
The lumped part behaves like the stub at every frequency.
Signal-flow loops can be added term by term (the coursework's Γin formula).

claims.why: Exact.

claims.claim: Move on the admittance circle first (shunt inductor), then on the 1 + jx circle (series capacitor)
claims.why: Because r = 1.44 > 1, a series part first only slides along the r = 1.44 circle, which never meets the g = 1 circle. Shunt-first is the only order that works; shunt L + series C is one of its two solutions (the other is shunt 1.20 pF + series 7.14 nH).
The step that lands exactly on the r = 1 circle is −0.096 (from y = 0.237 − j0.329 to 0.237 − j0.425). −0.12 is 25 % too big, a chart-reading error.
Exact value −1.794; −1.75 is within 2.5 %, normal for a paper chart. (The text labels the two steps the other way round, but the formulas use them correctly.)
The arithmetic from x = −1.75 is right (0.909 pF). The exact design value is 0.887 pF, 2.5 % away.
The arithmetic from b = −0.12 is right, but the reading is off: the exact value is 41.4 nH, so 33.16 nH is 20 % low. That is why the MWO dip sits at 2.025 GHz, not 2.000.

claims.claim: The MWO frequency response confirms a match at 2 GHz
claims.why: S11 at 2.000 GHz is −27.4 dB (0.18 % of the power reflected), so it is a usable match. But the dip is −27.8 dB at 2.025 GHz: the centre is pulled up by the 20 % low inductor. With 41.4 nH it is a perfect null at 2.000 GHz.
14.99 cm, so the 15 cm line is one wavelength.
Exact 3.51 cm (0.234λ).

claims.claim: Point A is 1 + j1.7, stub LA ≈ 1.29 cm (0.086λ)
claims.why: Exact y = 1 + j1.71 and ℓ = 1.26 cm (0.084λ). The MWO build gives −36.4 dB at 1.998 GHz, which this model reproduces to 0.01 dB.
Exact 5.57 cm (0.372λ).
Exact 6.23 cm (0.416λ). The MWO build gives −40.8 dB at 2.002 GHz, reproduced to 0.01 dB.

claims.claim: Two points (distances from the load) where the stub can be attached
claims.why: The two points given are right and are the ones nearest the load, which is what the question asks for. The 15 cm line is one wavelength, though, and the pattern repeats every λ/2: stubs at 11.0 cm and 13.1 cm match too.

claims.claim: Choose stub B: −40 dB is significantly lower than −36 dB
claims.why: The dip depth at one frequency only reflects how well the lengths were rounded; both are excellent matches. What differs is bandwidth: S11 < −10 dB from 1.842 to 2.180 GHz (337 MHz) for stub A, but only 1.916 to 2.064 GHz (148 MHz) for stub B. A is the better option: closer to the load and shorter, which the coursework's own closing paragraph says.

claims.claim: Zsc = +j30 Ω for stub A, so a shunt inductor replaces it; −j30 Ω for stub B, so a shunt capacitor

claims.why: 2.389 nH. MWO −36.2 dB at 1.998 GHz, reproduced.
2.66 pF from −j29.87 Ω; 2.65 pF comes from rounding to −j30. MWO −36.5 dB at 2.003 GHz, reproduced.
Exact.
Exact for Z = j30 Ω.
βl = 2π·0.115/0.15 = 4.817 rad (a decimal slip), and the phase term is e^(−jβl): without the j it is an attenuation, not a phase shift.

Loops do not add term by term. Evaluated with the right S-parameters it gives |Γin| = 0.256 at 2 GHz, against 0.016 (−35.9 dB) from the correct nested rule Γin = S11 + S12S21Γ′/(1 − S22Γ′) and from MWO.
All four reproduced.
